title: Sacred time (CCC 1163–1173)
hookLine: Sunday and the year make time holy

cards: A life can run on several calendars at once. Work time, with its deadlines. School time, with its terms.
Money time, with its paydays. Sports time, with its seasons and finals. The Catholic Church keeps another calendar running underneath them all.
Its week has a center. Its year has seasons with their own colors, purple, white, green, red, on the priest's vestments and the cloth on the altar. A family can go a long while without noticing it.

teach.b: Day one hundred forty-three gave the colors; today, what the calendar is for. First, the week has a center: Sunday. The Catechism calls it the Lord's Day, the day Christ rose.
John uses the same name in the Apocalypse, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day."

Sunday is both the first day of the week, the day creation began, and the eighth day, beyond the ordinary week, a sign of the new creation. It's when Catholics gather for Mass, a kind of weekly Easter.
Second, the year has a heart: Easter.
The Catechism calls it the feast of feasts, and quotes Saint Athanasius, who called it the Great Sunday. The light of the Easter days, it says, fills the whole year that follows.
Third, the year tells the whole story.
Around Easter, the Church walks through Christ's life: waiting in Advent, his birth at Christmas, his appearing to the nations, Lent's long walk toward the cross, and the weeks of Easter.

Alongside, it keeps feasts of Mary and memories of martyrs and saints, people who show Christ's Easter at work in real lives. Fourth, the word today. The liturgy keeps saying it: today Christ is born, today he is risen.
Not as if it's happening again, but because, Catholics believe, God's saving work isn't trapped in the past.
A psalm sung at Easter says it: "This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein." Sacred time is ordinary time, every day of it, given a shape and a center.

how: Catholics gather for Mass on Sundays and holy days, and follow the liturgical year's seasons, Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter and Ordinary Time, marked by readings and the colors of the priest's vestments.

games.q: the Church's year is like a wheel. which feast is its hub, the light that fills the rest?
games.why: the Catechism calls Easter the feast of feasts, and Athanasius called it the Great Sunday. its light fills the whole year.

practice: Ask where today sits in the Church's year: Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, or the long stretch the Church calls Ordinary Time.

Let the question itself slow you down, because today is not just a Tuesday or a Friday, it's one day in a story with a shape. If you pray, offer this day to God; if you don't, simply notice it as a day that won't come again.

wordCard.voice: Sacred time. Sunday, the Lord's Day, at the center of the week, and Easter, the feast of feasts, at the heart of the year, giving every ordinary day a shape. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: time made holy. Every ordinary day has a place in the story. Same time tomorrow.
